chapter: Early records, Detroit and Prohibition-era nightlife
title: Prohibition raids, gambling and buffet flats
summary: He was never in a raided place; he explains buffet flats as apartments where you could buy a drink, and the bootleg gin sold in them.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: You played in places like the Bamboo Inn, you know, this was all during Prohibition, and people brought their own liquor there and everybody was selling bootleg liquor there. Were you ever in places that were raided?

No, that's one thing, all my career, I was never in a place that was raided, never. They used to raid the -- in fact they'd raid most anyplace when they got ready. Even the Musicians' Club they used to raid. On any trumped up excuse, because they used to have gambling in the back room and all that. The Musicians' Club always had
gambling. They had poker tables and blackjack tables and whatever. But I was never in a room that was raided.
What about the buffet flats, what were they like?

Well, a buffet flat was where you went to eat, drink. Some of them were bawdy houses, you know. And it could be any house, a house like this, an apartment. An apartment, an apartment like this. And the standing joke was you could go in almost any apartment house and knock on almost any door and get something to drink, you know. You'd knock on the door and they'd say, "Who's there?" "Jimmy sent me." You know, okay, and he'd crack the door and look at you, and the thing I always marveled at -- I went through too, I used to do it, knock on the door, and he'd say to you, "What do you want, a pint?" You'd say yeah, and whatever he gave you you took. Whatever. You didn't specify anything in particular. Then later on the drink that became popular was shakeup gin, they used to call it. They used to have this gin, and I suppose the gangsters used to put it up. Of course you wouldn't get this in the average apartment, but it used to be -- the bottle used to say Gordon's Gin. It was wrapped up in yellow paper, you know. It cost one buck. Gordon's Gin.
